title: Questions Skeptics Ask: A Study for Doubters
subtitle: A five-session study for skeptics and seekers asking whether Christianity is true.
summary:
This study is for the person who doesn't believe, or isn't sure, and is willing to look anyway. It's also for the friend who invited them, who is about to find out how much harder it is to defend the faith than to assume it. Nothing here is a trick. There's no emotional ambush waiting in session five, no moment when the lights dim and you're asked to decide something you didn't come to decide. Each session takes one hard question, states the strongest case against Christianity first, and only then offers a response, and the response is allowed to be incomplete.

The five questions come in order: whether anyone is there at all; whether science has buried God; who Jesus actually was; whether the resurrection happened; and what kind of step faith is if the evidence doesn't force it. Along the way the study names serious thinkers on both sides, including C. S. Lewis, Alvin Plantinga, N. T. Wright, David Hume and Bart Ehrman, not to end the conversation but because they've done the work and are worth reading. A host who isn't an expert can lead it, and should say "I don't know" when that's true. No question is ever met with shame. Someone who asks the hard thing out loud is doing something brave, and the room exists to make that safe.
audience: Skeptics, seekers, agnostics, and the friends who invited them

sessions.title: Is There Anyone There
sessions.aim: To ask whether the universe is finally personal or finally empty, giving the case for atheism its full weight, and to put the arguments from fine-tuning and from morality on the table without claiming more than they show.
sessions.summary:
Before any question about Jesus or the Bible comes a prior one: is anyone there? Is the universe at bottom a someone or a vast, indifferent process?

The skeptic's position deserves to be stated strongly. In a scientific age the natural default is that no one is there: the cosmos is matter and energy running by fixed laws toward a cold end, and the longing for a someone behind it is the wishful thinking we'd expect from an animal that knows it will die. Against that, two arguments pull hard without proving anything. The first is fine-tuning: the basic constants of physics sit in ranges so narrow that small changes would leave a universe with no stars, no chemistry and no one to notice. Luck, an unobservable multiverse and a mind are all candidate explanations, and none can be directly proven. The second is the moral argument: we're convinced that cruelty is really wrong, not merely disliked, and that conviction is hard to ground in a universe that is only atoms. Neither forces belief. Together they make a personal universe a serious option.

keyScripture.why: An ancient claim that the order and grandeur of the world is a kind of speech pointing beyond itself, the intuition the fine-tuning question raises again in modern form.

discussion.q: Before tonight, when you imagined the universe at its deepest level, did you picture a someone or a something? Where did that picture come from?
discussion.behind: Bring the default into the open before arguing anything. Most people have never traced whether their picture came from reasoning, upbringing or the mood of the age. You're not settling it, only showing that it's an assumption. Go first if the room is slow.

discussion.q: The constants of physics sit in extremely narrow ranges that allow a universe with anyone in it. What's your first reaction to that? Does it move you at all?
discussion.behind: Get the gut response before the analysis. Some will reach for the multiverse right away; some will feel a pull they don't trust. Let people feel how strange the fact is, and notice how quickly they want to explain it away in either direction.

discussion.q: When you call something truly evil, what do you think you're claiming?
discussion.behind: This is the live wire. Press gently on whether moral judgments describe reality or express preference. Don't let it become a debate about whether atheists can be good people; obviously they can. Keep it on what grounds the "ought." Many of us live as if right and wrong are real and argue as if they aren't.

discussion.q: This study won't say these arguments prove God, only that they make a personal universe a serious option. Is that too modest, or is the modesty part of why it's worth hearing?
discussion.behind: Some in the room have been burned by apologetics that claimed too much. Let them see that an argument can be worth taking seriously without being a knockout, and that overclaiming is its own dishonesty.

discussion.q: Where do you notice your own wants pulling on what you find easy or hard to believe here?
discussion.behind: Make clear this cuts both ways. A skeptic may not want a God with a claim on him; a believer may want God for comfort. Nobody is being accused of bad faith. Desire shapes belief on every side, and saying so is where clear thinking starts. Go first.

objections.objection: Fine-tuning is no evidence. If the constants were different we wouldn't be here to notice, so of course we find ourselves in a universe that permits us. And a multiverse with every possible set of constants explains the tuning with no designer.
objections.response: Both halves have force. It's true that we could only find ourselves in a universe that permits us, but that doesn't explain why any such universe exists at all. A lottery winner can't be surprised that he's the one holding the ticket, but that doesn't mean there was no lottery. The multiverse is the more serious reply, and it's coherent. But notice its cost: it posits an immense, unobservable reality to avoid a designer, which is a vast commitment held without any laboratory result. So the fine-tuning is a real fact that calls for an explanation, and the main candidates, luck, a multiverse and a mind, each run past what can be directly proven. That doesn't prove God. It does mean the design inference is at least as respectable as its rivals, and a confident dismissal of it is a bluff.

objections.objection: Morality doesn't need God. Evolution and social contract explain it: cooperation helped our ancestors survive, so we evolved moral instincts, and societies built rules on top of them.
objections.response: That's very likely part of the true story, and a believer has no reason to deny it. But explaining why we feel that cruelty is wrong isn't the same as showing whether it is wrong. An account of how a belief arose says nothing about whether it's true. If our sense of justice is only a survival trick, then calling genocide evil reports a preference our genes installed, no truer than a taste for sugar. Most people can't live that way. They believe the torture of a child is really wrong. That doesn't prove God. But if real moral facts exist, facts that hold whether anyone agrees or not, they're very hard to ground in matter alone. The question is whether you can keep the conviction once you've removed what it stands on.

sessions.quietRoomQuestion: If it turned out someone is there, behind all of it, who knows your name, would that be the best news you've ever heard or the most unwelcome? What does your answer tell you?
sessions.practice: Run one experiment on your own mind this week. The next time you call something truly wrong, whether in the news or in your own past, stop and ask what you're claiming. Is it wrong the way a fashion rule is wrong, a custom? Or wrong the way two plus two isn't five, a fact? Write down which you actually believe when it matters, and whether your stated view and your lived conviction match.
sessions.closingPrayer: We'll close with a few words, and no one here has to agree with them. If you're there, and we aren't sure you are, we're asking to be shown what's true and not only what's comfortable. We know we want things, and that our wanting bends what we'll look at. Give us the courage to follow the evidence even where we'd rather it didn't go. If the heavens are saying anything, give us the patience to look up. Amen.
reflection: When I picture the universe at its deepest level, do I picture a someone or a something, and have I ever examined why?
When I call something truly evil, am I describing reality or reporting a preference, and can I live with the answer?
What do I want to be true about whether anyone is there, and how might that be shaping what I'll consider?
sessions.teaching:
Before we say anything about Jesus or the Bible or the church, we have to ask the question underneath them: is anyone there? Not whether religion is useful or faith is comforting, but whether the universe at its bottom is a person or a process, a someone or an indifferent machine running down toward the dark. Everything else in this study depends on that answer.

I want to state the skeptic's position at full strength, because it was mine. I came to faith from atheism, and I won't caricature a view I held. The natural default of an educated, scientific age is that no one is there. The cosmos is matter and energy, governed by fixed laws, running from a hot beginning toward a cold end, and it doesn't know we exist. The craving for a someone behind it all, a Father or a mind or a meaning, is exactly the wishful projection you'd predict from a clever, frightened animal that has just become smart enough to know it will die. That isn't a stupid position. Serious people hold it, and if you hold it, you're welcome here as you are.

Two things pull against it, and I want to be careful with both, because the fastest way to lose a thinking person is to claim more than you can deliver.

The first is what physicists call fine-tuning. Over the last century we've learned that several basic constants of nature, such as the strength of gravity and the force that binds atomic nuclei, sit within remarkably narrow ranges. Change some of them slightly and you don't get a different universe with different life. You get a universe with no stars, no chemistry and no observers. That doesn't prove God, and anyone who says it does is selling something. There are real replies. We could only ever find ourselves in a universe that permits us. Or perhaps there are countless universes with every possible setting, and we're in one of the rare livable ones. Both are coherent. But the first doesn't explain why any livable universe exists, and the second avoids a designer by positing an immense, unobservable ocean of universes, which is a large act of faith in its own right. Fine-tuning is a real fact that calls for explanation, and every explanation on the table runs past what can be directly proven. The design inference isn't the embarrassing relic our age assumes.

The second is the moral argument, and it doesn't let go. We don't merely dislike cruelty. We believe it's wrong. When we read of a child tortured for someone's pleasure, we don't think "not to my taste." We think "evil," and we think it would still be evil if everyone alive approved. That conviction has the texture of a fact, something discovered rather than invented. The atheist has a good account of where the feeling came from: evolution wired us for cooperation, and culture built rules on the wiring. A Christian needn't deny a word of that. But explaining how we came to feel that cruelty is wrong doesn't establish that it is wrong. If our deepest moral convictions are only survival tricks, then calling genocide evil is reporting a feeling. Almost no one can live that way. C. S. Lewis, who also came to faith from unbelief, built the opening of Mere Christianity on this: the strange authority of the "ought," the sense that we answer to a law we didn't make. If real moral facts exist, a personal universe explains them more naturally than an impersonal one.

So I won't overclaim, and I won't let us underclaim either. Neither argument forces belief. Together they make a personal universe a serious, intellectually respectable option. Paul argued the same way in Athens, from creation and conscience rather than from a Bible his hearers didn't accept (Acts 17:24-28).

One last thing, and it applies to all of us. Part of why some people hold the no-one-there view tightly is that they want it, because a someone behind the universe would have a claim on them. Believers aren't exempt; wanting God to exist for comfort is its own distortion. Thinking clearly starts with admitting the pull. So that's the question tonight. Not whether it's proven, but whether anyone is there, and whether you've let yourself ask with your mind fully engaged and your wants out on the table.

scriptureStudy.note: "The heavens declare the glory of God." The physical order as a kind of speech pointing past itself, the old form of the intuition fine-tuning raises.
God's "eternal power and divine nature" are "clearly perceived... in the things that have been made." Paul treats creation as evidence open to anyone, ground a skeptic can examine.
The law "written on their hearts, while their conscience also bears witness." A moral knowledge built into people, the thing the moral argument tries to account for.
Paul tells Athenian philosophers that God "is actually not far from each one of us," quoting their own poets. He argues on shared ground.

"The fool says in his heart, 'There is no God.'" The Hebrew fool is the one who lives as if the question doesn't matter, a moral posture rather than a lack of intelligence. The verse is aimed at indifference, not at someone weighing the question.
"He has put eternity into man's heart." The sense that we're made for more than the visible.
"What is seen was not made out of things that are visible." The visible world rests on an invisible cause, which is the design question stated plainly.

sessions.goingDeeper:
These questions belong to what philosophers call natural theology: reasoning toward God from the world rather than from Scripture. Thomas Aquinas, writing in the thirteenth century, framed arguments from causation and contingency: why is there something rather than nothing, and can a chain of dependent things hang on nothing at all? Fine-tuning is a new chapter in that old line.

On the other side, read David Hume's Dialogues Concerning Natural Religion (published in 1779, after his death). His criticisms of the design argument remain among the sharpest ever written, and a believer should read them before calling the matter settled. Among contemporary voices, set William Lane Craig on the cosmological and moral arguments, and Alvin Plantinga on whether belief in God can be rational without proof, beside their critics. The debate is live, carried on by capable people on both sides. Resist two temptations: the believer's, to treat these arguments as proofs, and the skeptic's, to treat them as long-refuted embarrassments. Neither is accurate. They raise the probability without compelling assent, and where the evidence stops a decision begins, which is where session five goes.
sessions.caseStudy:
Suppose a graduate student comes to the group certain no one is there. He says so in the first ten minutes: the universe is matter and energy, and meaning is something humans paint on it.

The host doesn't argue. He raises fine-tuning and watches the student reach for the multiverse, which is a responsible move. Then he asks gently whether positing countless unobservable universes to avoid a designer is itself a kind of faith. Later, on the moral argument, the student says cruelty is wrong because it causes suffering, and the host asks whether suffering is wrong as a matter of fact or as a matter of preference. The student, being truthful, says he believes it's really wrong and can't fully say why on his own view.

He may leave no more convinced of God, but having noticed that his certainty was less examined than he thought. That's what the session is for. The host didn't win. He helped a thinking person see his own assumptions.

sessions.title: Hasn't Science Buried God
sessions.aim: To take the supposed war between science and faith at full strength, then show that it's largely an inherited story, and to separate what science establishes from the philosophy often carried in beside it.
sessions.summary:
Everyone knows the story. Religion kept the world in superstitious darkness, science arrived with evidence, the two went to war, and science won. Parts of it are true: the church has at times resisted new knowledge.

But is it true as history? Historians of science now largely regard the grand "warfare" story as a nineteenth-century creation, popularized by John William Draper (1874) and Andrew Dickson White (1896). Much of modern science grew among believers who expected an orderly world because they believed in an orderly Creator. And there's a deeper confusion. Science tells you how the mechanism works. It's silent on whether there's a maker or meaning behind it, because its instruments aren't built to reach that question. The strongest objection is the "god of the gaps," a God who shrinks every time science explains something new. That danger is real, and believers should reject that god too. But the Christian claim was never that God is one cause among natural causes. It's that he's the reason there's a lawful universe to study at all.

keyScripture.why: God isn't a gap in the natural order but the ground of the whole order, the distinction that dissolves the supposed war between science and faith.

discussion.q: Where did you first get the idea that science and religion are at war? Was it ever argued to you, or just assumed?
discussion.behind: The war story is usually absorbed from school, film and the general air rather than reasoned through. Let the room notice they hold a strong historical claim they've never checked.

discussion.q: The church really has resisted knowledge at times. What examples come to mind? Does naming them make the deeper question easier or harder to discuss?
discussion.behind: Concede what's true before disputing what isn't. Let people name Galileo or whatever they carry. Showing that the study isn't defensive earns the right to question the larger story.

discussion.q: Read Colossians 1:16-17. Science tells you how the mechanism works but is silent on whether there's a maker behind it. Does that distinction seem fair to you, or like a way of protecting faith from evidence?
discussion.behind: This is the likeliest place for pushback. Some will hear a dodge that puts God out of reach of testing. Let them say so. Then help the room see the difference between a claim science can't reach and a claim science has refuted.

discussion.q: Have you seen faith used as a "god of the gaps," invoked for whatever science hasn't yet explained? Why is that a bad argument even for a believer?
discussion.behind: Concede the strongest form of the objection openly. A god invoked only to plug ignorance does retreat with every discovery. Separate that bad argument from the claim that God grounds the whole lawful order.

discussion.q: Many founders of modern science, such as Kepler, Boyle and Newton, were believers who expected an orderly world from an orderly maker. Does that surprise you? What does the surprise say about the story we were handed?
discussion.behind: Keep a light touch. The point isn't to score but to notice how much of what we're sure of turns out to be received rather than examined, on every side, believers included.

objections.objection: Science and religion are at war and science keeps winning. Every time we said "God did it," whether lightning, disease or the origin of species, science found the natural cause. God is just the name for what we can't yet explain, and that territory shrinks every year.
objections.response: There's a real part to this. People have invoked God for events that later got natural explanations, and a faith that lives only in the gaps of current science is bound to shrink. A believer should reject that god as firmly as any atheist. But the historic Christian claim was never that God is one more cause inside the chain, competing with germs for the same job. It's that God is the author of the whole chain, the reason there's a lawful universe in which lightning has causes at all. Discovering how an engine works doesn't eliminate the engineer. Science describes the mechanism. Whether the mechanism has an author is a different kind of question, and no description of the mechanism can answer it.

objections.objection: If God is real, that should be testable, and it isn't. You've defined God as something science can never touch, which is exactly what you'd do to protect a belief from being disproven.
objections.response: That deserves a straight answer. First, many things we rightly believe aren't testable by natural science: that other minds exist, that the past was real and the world wasn't created five minutes ago with false memories, that torturing the innocent is wrong, that the laws of logic hold. Science itself rests on assumptions it can't test, such as the reliability of reason and the uniformity of nature. The rule that every serious claim must be scientifically testable can't pass its own test. Second, the Christian claim isn't wholly untestable. It makes historical claims, about a man who lived, died and whose tomb was found empty, which the next two sessions examine. It's protected only from a single method never designed to address it.

sessions.quietRoomQuestion: If the war between science and faith turned out to be a story you inherited rather than a fact you established, what else you're sure of might be inherited rather than examined?
sessions.practice: Pick one claim you've always assumed was settled science against faith, whether the war itself or the idea that no serious scientist believes, and spend thirty minutes on its history this week. Read someone competent on each side, not a meme. Write down whether the claim held up as well as you assumed, and how it felt to examine something you were sure of.
sessions.closingPrayer: We'll close, and you're free to listen as an observer. If you're the author of this orderly world and not a gap in our knowledge of it, we confess how easily we mistake the description of the mechanism for the whole truth. Give us the discipline to know what our methods can reach and what they can't, and the humility to stop calling a philosophy a finding. Where we've been handed a story and called it knowledge, on any side, show us the difference. Amen.
reflection: Where did I get the idea that science and faith are at war, and have I examined whether the history supports it?
Can I tell a claim science has refuted from a claim science was never built to reach?
Which beliefs do I hold that aren't scientifically testable, and do I treat them as unserious, or quietly make an exception?
sessions.teaching:
We all grew up inside the story. Religion held the human race in superstitious darkness, teaching that the earth was the center and disease was a curse. Then science arrived with telescopes and evidence, the two went to war, and science won battle after battle until God was left as a comfort for people who can't face the facts. It's told in classrooms and films, and if you believe it you aren't a fool, because parts of it are true. The church has at times resisted new knowledge, and there have been real fights and real censorship in the name of faith. I won't pretend otherwise.

But two harder questions are worth asking. Is the war story true as history? And does science, rightly understood, bury God?

Start with the history, because it surprises people. The idea of an age-old war between science and religion was popularized by two nineteenth-century books: John William Draper's History of the Conflict Between Religion and Science (1874) and Andrew Dickson White's A History of the Warfare of Science with Theology in Christendom (1896). Both were enormously popular, and their thesis became the water we swim in. Later historians of science largely took it apart. David Lindberg spent a career showing that the medieval period was full of churchmen doing serious natural philosophy. In 2009 Ronald Numbers edited a collection called Galileo Goes to Jail and Other Myths about Science and Religion, examining the legends one by one. Among historians of science today, believing and unbelieving, the Draper and White thesis isn't a live position.

The record those historians recovered tells a different story. Much of modern science grew among believers, and not by accident. Figures like Kepler, Boyle and Newton understood their work as studying God's creation. They expected the natural world to be orderly and intelligible because they believed it was the work of an orderly, intelligent Creator. That doesn't prove Christianity, but it does undo the simple story that faith and science are natural enemies.

Now the substance. Science studies the mechanism. It asks how: how the heart pumps, how species change, how the universe expanded. These are magnificent achievements, and a Christian should celebrate every one. But science, by its method, is silent on whether there's a meaning or a maker behind the mechanism, because its instruments aren't built for that question. To say there's no God because science hasn't found one is like saying there's no author because you read the whole novel and found only sentences. The author is the reason there's a story at all, present on every page and visible on none of them the way a character is. Paul puts the Christian claim this way: "in him all things were created... and in him all things hold together" (Colossians 1:16-17).

The strongest objection is the god of the gaps: whatever science can't yet explain, believers say God did it, and then science explains it and God shrinks. The skeptic is right about that god. A god who lives only in the gaps of current knowledge is doomed, and a thinking believer should reject him too. But God was never proposed as one cause among others, competing with germs for the job of making people sick. The claim is that he's the reason there's a lawful universe in which germs have predictable effects. Understanding an engine doesn't eliminate the engineer.

The sharpest form is this: if God is real, it should be testable, and you've conveniently defined God as the one thing science can't touch. Here's a straight answer. Many things we rightly believe can't be tested by natural science: that other people have minds, that the past actually happened, that torturing the innocent is wrong, that the laws of logic hold. Science itself stands on beliefs it can't test, such as the reliability of reason and the uniformity of nature. The rule that only testable claims are serious isn't itself testable. It's a philosophy.

And the Christian claim doesn't float beyond all evidence. It plants itself in history: a particular man lived, was executed under a named Roman official, and was found alive again, his followers insisted, with his tomb empty. That invites investigation, and we'll spend the next two sessions doing it. The real argument was never between science and God. It's between two philosophies, one that says the mechanism is all there is and one that says it has a maker, and only one of them has learned to wear a lab coat in public as though it belonged to it.

scriptureStudy.note: "In him all things hold together." God as the ground of the whole order rather than one cause inside it.
"In the beginning, God created the heavens and the earth." A claim about authorship and origin. It answers who and why, and leaves the how to investigation.
"Great are the works of the LORD, studied by all who delight in them." Studying the natural world is commended as delight, not feared as a threat.
"It is the glory of God to conceal things, but the glory of kings is to search things out." Investigation is dignified, the searching out of a world made to be searched.
"Where were you when I laid the foundation of the earth?" God answers Job by showing the order and size of creation.
God's power and nature are "clearly perceived... in the things that have been made." The made world is open to reason, which is why a believer welcomes investigation.
"In him we live and move and have our being." God isn't a being inside the universe to be located by instruments.

sessions.goingDeeper:
Look at the actual history of the so-called conflict. Read Draper and White, then read historians of science such as David Lindberg and Ronald Numbers, who show that the relationship between Christianity and the rise of science was far more often cooperation than combat. Even the famous flashpoints, Galileo above all, were tangled in politics, personality and patronage at least as much as in any clean clash of faith against evidence.

Then press the other direction, so the conversation doesn't turn triumphant: where have Christians really obstructed inquiry and earned the suspicion? The discipline is to separate three things the war story fuses: the real and sometimes shameful history of particular conflicts; the manufactured myth of an ancient, essential warfare; and the open philosophical question of whether the success of science supports or undercuts belief in God. The first is settled, the second is false, and the third is still being argued.
sessions.caseStudy:
Suppose a retired engineer joins the group because her son told her science had made faith obsolete, and she wants to understand what he means. She repeats what she's absorbed: no serious scientist believes anymore, and the two have always been at war.

The host grants that the church has sometimes resisted knowledge, and she relaxes, because she expected defensiveness. Then he asks where she first heard the war story, and she realizes she can't remember it ever being argued, only assumed. Someone mentions that many founders of modern science were believers. She says she'd want to check that before accepting it, and the host says that's exactly the right instinct.

She leaves with homework she chose herself: examining a story she'd held as fact. The session was never meant to recruit her. It was to show her she'd been carrying a conclusion she hadn't examined.
