sessions.title: Who Was Jesus, Really
sessions.aim: To move from God in general to the man from Nazareth, taking the skeptical accounts of Jesus seriously, and to face the old, underrated problem of what he claimed about himself.
sessions.summary:
Almost everyone admires Jesus. Skeptics and believers often agree he was a great moral teacher. That shared admiration is where the trouble starts, because the gentle teacher of popular imagination isn't quite the man the earliest sources describe.

The skeptical options deserve a full hearing. Maybe the real Jesus was a wise teacher whose followers later inflated him. Maybe the divine claims are legends that grew over generations. Serious scholars hold these views. But the sources we have show a man who forgave sins committed against other people, claimed authority over the Sabbath, accepted worship, and was condemned for blasphemy. C. S. Lewis put the dilemma sharply: a man who said such things doesn't leave us the option of calling him merely a great teacher. The legend theory has to reckon with how early and how Jewish the highest claims are. The session doesn't tell you which answer to choose. It suggests that the easy answer may be the one the man himself ruled out.

keyScripture.why: The scribes react as careful monotheists would: "Who can forgive sins but God alone?" The highest claim about Jesus sits in the earliest layer of the sources, and those who heard it understood it.

discussion.q: Before tonight, who was Jesus in your mind? How much of that picture came from the sources and how much from the culture around you?
discussion.behind: Most people hold a Jesus assembled from films, holidays and goodwill. Bring out the gap between the inherited figure and the documented one, gently, without implying anyone's been foolish.

discussion.q: Many skeptics and believers agree Jesus was a great moral teacher. Why might that be the hardest position to hold once you read the sources?
discussion.behind: This is the hinge. The shared admiration feels safe. Let the room feel the pressure Lewis named: a man making these claims can't easily be filed under "merely wise."

discussion.q: Take the legend theory seriously: the divine claims grew over time. What would have to be true for that to work, and what about the timing of the sources makes it harder?
discussion.behind: Give the skeptical view its strongest form, then test it. Legends need time. The difficulty is how early the highest claims appear, among Jews for whom worshiping a man was unthinkable.

discussion.q: Lewis argued that a man claiming what Jesus claimed is either a liar, a lunatic or Lord, not merely a fine teacher. Where do you feel the force of that, and where do you want to resist it?
discussion.behind: Let people push on it, including at its real weak point: it assumes Jesus made the claims, which the legend theory disputes. The aim isn't to call the argument airtight but to feel its force once the sources are granted.

discussion.q: Where do you keep something at the level of admiration so it can't make a claim on you?
discussion.behind: Admiring Jesus can be a way to avoid deciding about him. This is common, and the leader should own a version of it. Go first.

objections.objection: The divine Jesus is a legend. The historical man was a wise teacher or a failed prophet, and over decades his followers inflated him into a god. The miracles and divine claims are later additions.
objections.response: This has serious defenders, so weigh it rather than wave it off. Legends do grow. But legends need time, and the time doesn't seem to be there. Paul's letters, written in the 50s, already speak of Jesus in the highest terms and pass on creedal material that many scholars, skeptical ones included, date to within a few years of the crucifixion (1 Corinthians 15:3-5; compare Philippians 2:6-11). And these claims arose among first-century Jews, fierce monotheists for whom worshiping a human being was the gravest sin, the least likely soil for a quick man-made god. N. T. Wright has written at length on how strange that is. The legend theory doesn't vanish, but it has to explain a very large effect in a very short time among the people least disposed to produce it.

objections.objection: Claiming to be divine doesn't make you divine. Plenty of people have claimed to be God or to speak for him, and they were deluded or manipulative. Why should Jesus get a different verdict?
objections.response: That's fair, and the trilemma alone doesn't answer it, because "liar" and "lunatic" have to be weighed, not dismissed. The lunatic option has to account for the rest of the portrait: the moral depth, the steadiness under pressure, teaching that has commanded respect for two thousand years. The liar option has to explain why a deceiver would hold to a message that led to his execution, and why his closest followers, who would have known, kept proclaiming it at great cost. Neither is impossible, and a thoughtful skeptic can land on one. But the verdict that takes no work, the nice teacher, is the one the sources make hardest.

sessions.quietRoomQuestion: If Jesus said and meant what the earliest sources record, admiring him as a great teacher is no longer available. Which of the remaining options would you least want to be true, and why that one?
sessions.practice: Read the Gospel of Mark straight through this week, which takes about ninety minutes, the way you'd read any short ancient biography. Mark every place where Jesus says or does something a merely wise teacher wouldn't: forgiving sins, accepting worship, speaking with authority over the law. Write down whether the man on the page matches the gentle teacher of popular imagination, and where he doesn't.
sessions.closingPrayer: We'll close plainly, and you're welcome only to listen. If you were who the earliest witnesses said you were, we've often kept you at the safe distance of admiration so we wouldn't have to face the harder question. Give us the courage to read the sources rather than the convenient picture, and to let the man on the page be as strange and demanding as he is. Show us who you really were. Amen.
reflection: How much of my picture of Jesus comes from the earliest sources, and how much from the culture around me?
If the gentle-teacher view is the hardest to hold once I read the texts, what work has it been doing for me?
Among liar, lunatic and Lord, which would I least want to be true, and have I avoided choosing to avoid that one?
sessions.teaching:
Christianity doesn't finally rest on an argument from physics or philosophy. It rests on a person, a first-century Galilean Jew named Jesus of Nazareth, and the only way forward is to ask who he actually was.

Here's what makes this the most interesting of our five questions. Almost everyone admires him. The skeptic and the believer in this room probably agree that Jesus was a remarkable moral teacher, a champion of the poor, a person of rare compassion. That agreement feels like common ground, and it is. It's also where the trouble starts, because the gentle teacher we all admire isn't quite the man the earliest sources describe.

Take the skeptical options first. One says the real Jesus was a wise teacher whose followers later draped a divine costume over him. Another says the divine claims are legend that grew over generations. These are defended by capable scholars, and holding one isn't foolish; it's looking for the most ordinary explanation of an extraordinary set of texts.

But the gentle-teacher view has always had something hard to swallow. The sources we have don't give us a modest sage offering tips for living. When a paralyzed man is lowered through a roof, Jesus says, "Son, your sins are forgiven," and the scribes object, "Who can forgive sins but God alone?" (Mark 2:5-7). You can forgive what's done to you. Forgiving a stranger's sins against others is standing in God's place, and the people watching understood that at once. Jesus claimed that "the Son of Man is lord even of the Sabbath" (Mark 2:28). He said, "I and the Father are one" (John 10:30), and "before Abraham was, I am" (John 8:58), echoing the name God gave Moses. And he was condemned at last not for teaching kindness, which gets no one crucified, but because the high priest heard his answer as blasphemy (Mark 14:61-64).

C. S. Lewis put the matter in a form that has gripped and annoyed readers ever since. A man who said the things Jesus said, he argued in Mere Christianity, wouldn't be a great moral teacher. He'd be a lunatic, or something worse, or else exactly who he claimed to be. Lewis ends with the warning: "let us not come with any patronising nonsense about His being a great human teacher. He has not left that open to us. He did not intend to."

Now the legend theory deserves a real test. Legends do grow. But they need time for a teacher to ripen into a god, and the time doesn't seem to be there. Paul's letters, written in the 50s, already speak of Jesus in the highest terms, and they pass on creedal material that many scholars, skeptical ones included, date to within a few years of the crucifixion (1 Corinthians 15:3-5). The hymn in Philippians 2:6-11, which many think predates the letter, speaks of Jesus as being "in the form of God." And this happened among first-century Jews, the fiercest monotheists of the ancient world, for whom worshiping a human being was unthinkable. That's the least promising soil for a man-made god to grow quickly. N. T. Wright has given much of his career to this puzzle. The legend theory doesn't simply collapse, but it now has to explain a very large effect in a very short time among the people least likely to produce it.

So weigh the options. Perhaps he was deluded about himself, though the rest of the portrait, the moral insight and the steadiness under pressure, is a strange profile for that. Perhaps he was a deceiver, though the message cost him his life, and his closest friends, who'd have known, kept proclaiming it at great cost. Neither is impossible, and a skeptic can plant a flag on one and I'll respect it. But notice what has happened. The verdict that costs nothing, the nice teacher, is the one the evidence makes hardest to hold.

Many of us, believers included, admire Jesus so that we won't have to decide about him. You can applaud a teacher and walk away. A Lord has a claim on you. Jesus asked his own disciples, "But who do you say that I am?" (Matthew 16:15). We don't have to answer tonight. But read the sources, not the inherited picture, and you may find that the comfortable middle ground is the one patch of ground he dug out from under us.

scriptureStudy.note: "Who can forgive sins but God alone?" Careful monotheists recognize a divine claim, in the earliest layer of the sources.
Jesus' answer to the high priest is heard as blasphemy, and he's condemned for it. He dies for a claim about his identity, not for teaching kindness.
"I and the Father are one." The crowd responds, "you, being a man, make yourself God." Those who heard it took it as a claim to deity.
"Before Abraham was, I am." An echo of the divine name in Exodus 3:14, and again the hearers pick up stones.
"But who do you say that I am?" Jesus presses the identity question on his own followers and won't let it stay abstract.
Jesus, "though he was in the form of God," is given "the name that is above every name." Many scholars think this hymn predates the letter, which counts against slow legendary growth.
A creed of Christ's death and resurrection that Paul "received" and handed on, dated by many scholars to within a few years of the events.

sessions.goingDeeper:
Scholars have pursued the historical Jesus for more than two centuries. Nineteenth-century attempts often produced a Jesus suspiciously like the scholars writing them. Much of the mid-twentieth century doubted how much could be known at all. More recent work places Jesus firmly within first-century Judaism.

Read across the range. On the skeptical side, the Jesus Seminar of the 1980s and 1990s argued that most sayings attributed to Jesus are later developments, and Bart Ehrman's How Jesus Became God (2014) traces how, in his view, Jesus came to be called divine. On the other side, N. T. Wright's multivolume work places Jesus in Second Temple Judaism and argues that his self-understanding and the rise of resurrection belief fit something close to the church's account, and Richard Bauckham's Jesus and the Eyewitnesses (2006) argues that the Gospels rest on named eyewitness testimony. Weigh the criteria historians use, such as multiple attestation and embarrassment, and where they're strong and where they're contested. Resist both the popular skeptical confidence that the historical Jesus is unknowable and the apologetic temptation to make the sources tidier than they are.
sessions.caseStudy:
Suppose a man raised vaguely religious and now firmly secular tells the group he admires Jesus enormously, the teaching about the poor, the forgiveness, the courage, and that's exactly why he resents Christians for turning a good man into a god.

The host thanks him and asks him to do one thing before next time: read Mark straight through and mark every place where Jesus says or does something a merely wise teacher wouldn't. He comes back unsettled. He hadn't noticed how often Jesus forgives sins, accepts worship and claims authority over the law, and he says, a little frustrated, that the gentle teacher is harder to find on the page than he expected.

The host doesn't pounce. He names the situation Lewis named and asks which of the remaining options the man finds least believable, and why. He isn't converted. For the first time he's reckoning with the man instead of the picture, which is all the session set out to do.

memoryVerse.text: He said to them, "But who do you say that I am?"

sessions.title: Did the Resurrection Happen
sessions.aim: To treat the central claim of Christianity as a historical question, take the natural explanations at full strength, and weigh the facts most historians grant against the explanations on offer.
sessions.summary:
Christianity stakes everything on one event and says so: "if Christ has not been raised, then our preaching is in vain and your faith is in vain" (1 Corinthians 15:14). That's an odd thing for a religion to put in writing unless it means to be checked.

So this session works as a historian works. The natural explanations come first: the disciples stole the body; they had grief visions; Jesus didn't really die; it's all later legend. Each deserves a fair hearing. Then comes the "minimal facts" approach associated with Gary Habermas, which builds only on data that most scholars of the period grant, skeptics included. Jesus died by crucifixion. His followers sincerely believed they'd seen him alive and were changed by it. The persecutor Paul and the skeptic James were turned by what they took to be appearances. And the preaching began in Jerusalem, where a body could have ended it. Each natural theory strains against one fact or another. The session doesn't call the case closed. It calls it real.

keyScripture.why: Paul stakes the whole faith on a public event and refuses any symbolic escape, which is why the resurrection can be examined as evidence and not only believed as doctrine.

discussion.q: Read 1 Corinthians 15:12-19. What do you make of a faith that stakes everything on one historical claim?
discussion.behind: Most people assume religion is private feeling, immune to facts. Let the room notice that this faith volunteered to be falsifiable, which invites exactly the scrutiny this session applies.

discussion.q: Before weighing any evidence, how unlikely does a resurrection seem to you? Does that starting point settle the question before the evidence is heard?
discussion.behind: Someone certain miracles are impossible has decided the case before opening the file. Don't try to dislodge anyone's starting point. Just help people see that it's doing work, and ask whether it came from evidence or was held in advance.

discussion.q: Most scholars, including skeptics, grant the death, the disciples' sincere belief in appearances, the conversions of Paul and James, and the early preaching in Jerusalem. Which of those surprises you most?
discussion.behind: Many assume skeptics deny everything. Establish the shared ground first, so the question becomes what best explains the agreed facts.

discussion.q: Take the natural explanations one at a time: theft, hallucination, the swoon, legend. Which seems strongest to you, and where does it strain against an agreed fact?
discussion.behind: Give each its strongest form, then test it fairly. Let people defend the theories. This shouldn't be a rigged contest.

discussion.q: Where have you been certain about something precisely because you never examined it?
discussion.behind: This applies to the whole room, believers included. Certainty and investigation are different things. Go first.

objections.objection: Dead people stay dead. That's the most reliable fact we have, and no amount of old testimony can outweigh it. It's always more likely that the witnesses were mistaken, lying or legendary.
objections.response: This is the strongest objection, the one David Hume framed in 1748, and it's largely right. Dead people do stay dead; that's why a resurrection would be a miracle, and the witnesses knew it as well as we do, which is why they didn't believe it at first (Luke 24:11). The real question is whether the improbability is so total that no evidence could ever count. That's a philosophical claim, not a historical finding. If you've decided in advance that nothing outside nature can act within it, you've settled the case before reading a single source, and it's only fair to say so. If the question of whether anyone is there is still open, as session one argued, then the improbability is real but not infinite, and the evidence can at least be weighed.

objections.objection: The disciples sincerely believing they saw Jesus only proves they had experiences. Grief produces vivid visions of the dead all the time.
objections.response: Grieving people do sometimes have vivid experiences of the dead; that's well documented, and sincerity proves sincerity, not accuracy. But weigh how far that reaches. The sources report appearances to groups, including "more than five hundred brothers at one time" (1 Corinthians 15:6), and to James, who hadn't believed in his brother (John 7:5), and to Paul, who wasn't mourning a teacher but hunting a movement he hated. Visions don't empty a tomb, and they don't explain why the authorities in Jerusalem, with every motive to produce a body, apparently didn't. The hallucination theory explains some of the data well and some poorly, which is the situation with every natural theory here.

sessions.quietRoomQuestion: If the resurrection happened the way the witnesses said, everything Jesus claimed about himself was vindicated. Are you more afraid that it's false, or that it's true?
sessions.practice: Do what a historian or a juror would do. Read the resurrection accounts in all four Gospels and the creed in 1 Corinthians 15:3-8 side by side, and make two lists: where they agree and where they differ. Then ask whether the differences look like invention or like ordinary variation among witnesses describing the same event from different angles. Write down your verdict and your reason.
sessions.closingPrayer: We'll close, and you owe these words nothing. If it happened, if you were dead and then weren't, we ask for the willingness to follow the evidence on a question we'd rather keep closed. Take away the certainty we never earned, on any side. Where we're more afraid of the answer than eager for the truth, give us courage. And if the tomb was empty, don't let us refuse to look because of what we'd have to do about it. Amen.
reflection: How likely did I think a resurrection was before I looked, and did I reason my way there or start there?
Which natural explanation do I find strongest, and where does it strain against the facts most historians grant?
Am I more afraid that the resurrection is false or that it's true, and what does that tell me?
sessions.teaching:
Christianity is unusual in one respect, and it's the one that matters tonight. It stakes its whole truth on something that either happened in history or didn't, and it says so in writing from the start. Paul put it as bluntly as anyone could: "if Christ has not been raised, then our preaching is in vain and your faith is in vain.... If in Christ we have hope in this life only, we are of all people most to be pitied" (1 Corinthians 15:14, 19). He didn't call the resurrection a lovely symbol of renewal that stays true in your heart whatever happened to the body. He said that if the body stayed in the tomb, throw it all out and pity us. A faith that volunteers to be falsified is inviting you to check, so tonight we'll check.

An honest inquiry starts with the natural explanations, because reaching for the ordinary before the extraordinary is simply responsible. Maybe the disciples stole the body and lied. Maybe, crushed by grief, they had visions. Maybe Jesus didn't die on the cross but revived. Maybe the story is legend that grew in the retelling. Serious people have defended each of these, and each deserves a fair hearing.

First we need to agree on what we're explaining. The historian Gary Habermas is associated with what's called the minimal facts approach, and its discipline is worth respecting. It doesn't ask you to trust the Bible as God's word. It builds only on data granted by most scholars who study the period, including skeptics with no stake in the resurrection being true. Even on those strict terms, a short, stubborn list survives. First, Jesus died by Roman crucifixion, attested inside and outside the New Testament; the Roman historian Tacitus records that Christ "suffered the extreme penalty" under Pontius Pilate. Second, very soon afterward his followers sincerely believed they'd seen him alive, and some of them suffered and died for proclaiming it, which at least shows they weren't knowingly lying. Third, two men outside the movement were turned by what they took to be appearances: Paul, who had been persecuting the church (Acts 9:1-6), and Jesus' brother James, who earlier hadn't believed in him (John 7:5; 1 Corinthians 15:7). Fourth, the preaching began in Jerusalem within weeks (Acts 2:22-32), in the city where the execution happened, the one place where producing a body would have ended things.

Now run the natural theories against those facts. Theft runs against the second: people don't usually suffer and die for what they know they made up. Hallucination has real appeal, since grieving people do sometimes have vivid experiences of the dead. But it strains against appearances to groups, including "more than five hundred brothers at one time, most of whom are still alive" (1 Corinthians 15:6), a line that invited checking, and against the conversions of James and Paul, who weren't mourners primed to see a beloved teacher. Visions also don't empty tombs. The swoon theory asks us to believe that a man scourged, crucified and speared revived without care, moved the stone, and persuaded his followers he'd conquered death, when he'd have looked like a torture victim in desperate need of a doctor. And the legend theory runs into the wall from last session: the shortness of the time and the earliness of the creed.

I want to be fair, because this is where apologetics tends to overreach. I'm not saying the case is closed and only a fool resists. Each natural theory explains some of the data. Each also strains against at least one fact that even skeptics grant, and the resurrection, strange as it is, accounts for all four at once. So the question isn't whether you're compelled to believe. It's which explanation strains least, and whether you've actually asked.

Then the strongest objection, the one David Hume framed in 1748: dead people stay dead. That's largely right. It's why this would be a miracle and not a medical curiosity, and it's why the first witnesses didn't believe it either; Luke says the women's report "seemed to them an idle tale" (Luke 24:11). So the real question inside the objection is whether a resurrection is so improbable that no evidence could ever count. That isn't a historical finding. It's the philosophical commitment we looked at in session two, that nothing outside nature can act within it. If you've decided that in advance, the verdict came before the evidence. If the question of whether anyone is there is still open, the evidence is allowed into the room.

Many people, skeptics and believers alike, are sure about the resurrection without having examined it. So I won't ask you to believe tonight. I'll ask something smaller and harder: have you looked?

scriptureStudy.note: The early creed of death, burial, resurrection and appearances, including to more than five hundred at once, "most of whom are still alive." Paul names witnesses who could be questioned.
"If Christ has not been raised... your faith is in vain." Paul refuses any symbolic escape, which makes this a historical question.
The women find the tomb empty and flee, "for they were afraid." The earliest manuscripts of Mark end here, in fear rather than triumph, an awkward detail that reads more like memory than persuasion.
The risen Jesus invites them to touch him and eats fish. The account insists on a bodily resurrection, not a vision.
Thomas wants to see and touch before he'll believe, and Jesus meets him with evidence rather than rebuke.
Peter preaches the resurrection in Jerusalem within weeks, to people who'd seen the events, in the city where the body lay.
Saul, hunting the church, is stopped by what he's convinced is the risen Christ. An enemy's conversion is one of the facts any theory must explain.

sessions.goingDeeper:
Start with the philosophical question that governs everything. Read Hume's essay "Of Miracles" in An Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding (1748), then read responses arguing that his reasoning, taken strictly, would rule out any sufficiently unusual event regardless of evidence.

On the historical side, read Gary Habermas and Michael Licona's The Case for the Resurrection of Jesus (2004), which sets out the minimal facts approach, and Licona's longer The Resurrection of Jesus: A New Historiographical Approach (2010). Read Bart Ehrman as a careful scholar who grants that the disciples believed they saw Jesus while withholding the supernatural conclusion. Read N. T. Wright's The Resurrection of the Son of God (2003), which argues that the empty tomb and the appearances together, set against first-century Jewish beliefs, are best explained by an actual resurrection. Keep two questions apart: what the evidence supports, and what's possible in the first place. Much disagreement about the evidence is really disagreement about the second.
sessions.caseStudy:
Suppose a nurse who has watched many people die says flatly that the resurrection is impossible and no testimony could move her, because dead people stay dead. The host agrees completely, which surprises her, and says that's exactly why it would be a miracle and why the first witnesses didn't believe it either.

Then he asks: is your position that the evidence is weak, or that no evidence could ever count? She's careful, sees the difference, and admits it's the second, held before any source is read. The host lets that stand without attacking it, noting only that it's a philosophical commitment rather than a finding from the evidence.

Over the session she weighs the natural explanations against the agreed facts and concedes that each strains somewhere, while keeping her starting point. She leaves with her unbelief intact but clearer about where it comes from. The host treats that as a real and respectable result, because it is.

memoryVerse.text: And if Christ has not been raised, then our preaching is in vain and your faith is in vain.

sessions.title: The Leap That Is Not Blind
sessions.aim: To ask what kind of step faith is, taking seriously the charge that faith is belief without evidence, and to recover faith as warranted trust: commitment where the evidence points without proving, as in every other important part of life.
sessions.summary:
Four sessions have weighed evidence, and the result isn't a proof. It's a set of questions that point somewhere without forcing the conclusion. So what do you do with that?

The sharpest charge is that faith means believing without evidence, or against it: a leap in the dark. That describes a real kind of religion, and it deserves the criticism. But it isn't what faith means in its serious sense, and it isn't how anyone lives. In the New Testament the word means something close to trust, the reliance you place in someone you have reason to rely on. And everyone lives by trust that goes beyond proof. We trust that the world is real, that memory is roughly reliable, that the people we love aren't deceiving us. Marriage is the picture: you commit on evidence, not proof, and refusing to commit until proof arrives isn't rationality but a different and lonelier mistake. The evidence points. The question is no longer whether it's proven, but whether, given where it points, you're willing.

keyScripture.why: Faith is "assurance" and "conviction," not wishful ignorance: trust extended toward what isn't yet seen.

discussion.q: What did the word "faith" mean to you before tonight? Is that the meaning the serious tradition uses, or the one a certain kind of religion has earned for it?
discussion.behind: Many people hold the "believing without evidence" definition and assume every believer means that. Separate the word from its worst use, without dismissing why the bad definition exists.

discussion.q: Where have you seen faith used to mean believing against the evidence? Is it fair to judge all faith by that?
discussion.behind: Concede the legitimate target first; the study agrees the criticism lands on something real. Then ask whether the worst version is a fair definition of the whole. We wouldn't define science by its frauds.

discussion.q: Everyone trusts beyond proof: that the world is real, that memory works, that loved ones aren't deceiving us. Is that a fair use of the word "faith," or a trick to make everyone religious?
discussion.behind: Expect sharp pushback here, and welcome it. The point is real but limited: committing beyond strict proof is universal and reasonable, even if the things trusted differ in kind.

discussion.q: Where in your life have you reasonably committed before you had certainty?
discussion.behind: Make it concrete: marriage, friendship, trusting a doctor. Faith of this kind isn't foreign or irrational; it's how every important human commitment works.

discussion.q: Looking back over all five sessions, what question are you left holding tonight?
discussion.behind: Close without an ambush. Don't push anyone across a line. Invite each person, yourself included, to say where they actually are, which may be more open, more skeptical, or simply clearer than at the start. Go first.

objections.objection: Faith is believing without evidence. If you had evidence you'd call it knowledge. Calling it "warranted trust" just changes the definition when the original becomes inconvenient.
objections.response: There is a kind of religion that means exactly believing without evidence, that treats doubt as sin and questions as betrayal, and it has earned the criticism. A believer should be the first to reject it. But defining faith by its worst practitioners is like defining medicine by its quacks. The New Testament word translated "faith" means something close to trust or faithfulness, the reliance you place in someone you have reason to rely on. Peter tells Christians to be ready to give "a reason for the hope that is in you" (1 Peter 3:15), and Luke says he wrote so his reader could "have certainty" after careful investigation (Luke 1:1-4). And if trusting beyond proof is irrational, then so is trusting your senses, your memory and other minds, none of which you can prove without arguing in a circle. Faith isn't the opposite of evidence. It's what you do with evidence that points strongly without delivering mathematical certainty, which is to say, with almost everything that matters.

objections.objection: Even granting that, the warrant isn't strong enough. You've admitted the arguments don't prove God and the resurrection isn't certain. Committing my life to a probability is reckless. I'll wait until the evidence is conclusive.
objections.response: That's mostly right, and I'll say so. The evidence doesn't prove it. I've said that in every session, and I won't take it back now to win you. But look at the principle inside "I'll wait until it's conclusive." You don't live by it anywhere else. You didn't wait for proof before trusting the person you married or believing your memory of yesterday. In weighty human matters certainty doesn't arrive, and someone who won't commit until it does hasn't chosen safety. He's chosen to stand still, which is itself an answer. There's no neutral ground here. Withholding the step answers the question with a no while telling yourself you haven't answered. The real questions are which way the evidence points and whether you're willing to take the kind of step you take everywhere else.

sessions.quietRoomQuestion: You've committed to many important things without proof. What makes you demand a certainty here that you've never demanded anywhere else? Is the demand really about evidence, or about what you'd have to do if it were true?
sessions.practice: Take an inventory of your own faith this week, in the sense of trust, not religion. Write down five things you rely on every day that you can't prove: that other minds exist, that the past was real, that the future will resemble the past, that your reasoning can be trusted, that someone loves you. Notice that you commit to each on evidence that points without proving. Then ask whether the step the Christian claim asks for is a different kind of step, or the same kind toward a different object. Write down which.
sessions.closingPrayer: We'll close, and as in every session you owe these words nothing and may listen as a guest. We've spent five sessions thinking hard, and we haven't been handed proof, only evidence that points. So we ask for the willingness every important thing in life finally requires: to commit where the evidence leads rather than demand a certainty we ask for nowhere else. Where we've hidden behind a need for proof to avoid a step we're afraid of, show us gently. And if you're there, and if the tomb was empty, give us the courage to take the step with our eyes open. Amen.
reflection: Did I assume faith means believing without evidence, and have I confused the word with its worst examples?
Where have I committed before I had certainty, and why do I demand more proof here than anywhere else?
After five sessions, is my hesitation about the strength of the evidence, or about what I'd have to do if it were true?
sessions.teaching:
We've spent four sessions weighing real evidence on hard questions, and I owe you a clear account of where that leaves us. It hasn't handed us a proof. There's no argument at the end of session four so airtight that a thinking person couldn't walk away. What we have is a set of questions that point somewhere: a personal universe made a serious option by fine-tuning and the moral law; a war between science and faith that turns out to be mostly a story; a man whose own claims rule out the comfortable verdict of "nice teacher"; and a resurrection whose natural explanations each strain against facts the skeptics themselves grant. The evidence points. It doesn't march you across the line. So tonight is about what to do with a conclusion that is reasonable but not compelled.

The sharpest charge is that faith means believing without evidence, or against it, a decision to stop thinking, the opposite of reason. I'm not going to wave that away, because it describes something real. There's a kind of religion that means exactly that, that treats doubt as sin and questions as betrayal, and tells you to believe harder exactly where the reasons run thin. It's common, and it has earned the criticism. A thinking believer should be first in line to reject it.

But defining faith by that version is like defining medicine by its quacks. The New Testament word we translate "faith" means something close to trust or faithfulness, the reliance you place in someone you have good reason to rely on. Hebrews calls faith "the assurance of things hoped for, the conviction of things not seen" (Hebrews 11:1): assurance and conviction, not wishful ignorance. Luke opens his Gospel by saying he "followed all things closely for some time past" so that his reader "may have certainty concerning the things you have been taught" (Luke 1:3-4). The Bereans are praised for "examining the Scriptures daily to see if these things were so" (Acts 17:11). Faith in the serious sense isn't the absence of evidence. It's trust that goes beyond what can be strictly proven, toward what the evidence makes reasonable.

Seen that way, everyone lives by faith, the atheist as much as the believer. You trust that the world is real and not a simulation, and you can't prove it. You trust that your memory is roughly reliable. You trust that other people have minds and aren't sophisticated machines. You trust your own reasoning, using reason to defend reason. None of these is provable, all of them are reasonable, and you couldn't get out of bed without them.

Marriage shows the structure clearly. Two people commit to a lifetime without proof. What they have is evidence: character, history, knowledge of each other. At some point they commit beyond what the evidence can prove, because the evidence invites it. Someone who says "I won't marry you until I'm certain you'll never leave" hasn't chosen the safe, rational path. That certainty never comes, and the waiting is itself a verdict, a no dressed up as caution.

The philosopher Alvin Plantinga has argued, most fully in Warranted Christian Belief (2000), that belief in God can be rational without being the conclusion of an argument, much as belief in other minds is. If he's right, the demand that faith be the airtight result of a proof may have been the wrong demand from the start. In the nineteenth century W. K. Clifford insisted, "It is wrong always, everywhere, and for anyone, to believe anything upon insufficient evidence," and William James replied in The Will to Believe (1896) that some real, unavoidable choices have to be made before the evidence is complete. You can weigh them for yourself.

So here's where five sessions leave us, and I won't tie a bow on it, because manufacturing a decision now would break every promise this study made. What's in front of you isn't a leap in the dark. It's the kind of step you take in every important thing, made with your eyes open. The question is no longer whether it's proven, because almost nothing that matters is. It's whether, given where the evidence points, you're willing.

One last thing, because I promised no trick. Many people tell themselves their unbelief is about the evidence. Some eventually find that what holds them back isn't the weakness of the case but the cost of the conclusion, what it would ask of a life they want to keep. Jesus said, "If anyone's will is to do God's will, he will know whether the teaching is from God" (John 7:17). I'm not saying that's true of you. Your hesitation may be entirely sincere, and if it is, this room honors it, and you can leave still weighing, with no ambush at the door. But it's worth asking yourself: is it the evidence, or what you'd have to do if it were true?

scriptureStudy.note: "The assurance of things hoped for, the conviction of things not seen." Confident trust toward what isn't yet visible, not belief against evidence.
Thomas is given what he asks for. Doubt is met with evidence, and the blessing on those who believe without seeing commends trust beyond sight, not belief without reason.
Luke investigated so that his reader "may have certainty." The Gospel presents itself as the fruit of inquiry, written for someone who wants to check.
"Always being prepared to make a defense to anyone who asks you for a reason for the hope that is in you." Faith has reasons that can be stated.
"I believe; help my unbelief!" Faith and doubt held together in a single sentence, which is the shape of trust that goes beyond certainty.
The Bereans examined the Scriptures daily "to see if these things were so," and they're called noble for it.
"If anyone's will is to do God's will, he will know." Knowing is tied to willingness: at some point the obstacle may be the will rather than information.

sessions.goingDeeper:
The relationship between faith and reason has been argued for centuries. At one end is evidentialism, put sharply by W. K. Clifford in "The Ethics of Belief" (1877): "It is wrong always, everywhere, and for anyone, to believe anything upon insufficient evidence." William James answered in The Will to Believe (1896) that some live, forced choices have to be made before the evidence is complete. Alvin Plantinga's reformed epistemology argues that belief in God can be "properly basic," rational without being inferred from other beliefs, the way belief in other minds is.

Weigh the long tradition that sees faith and reason as allies, summed up in Anselm's phrase "faith seeking understanding," against the strands of thought, some of them Christian, that set them against each other. Ask whether the demand that every belief be proven can meet its own standard. And notice that no question that matters most in a human life, in love, in vocation, in trusting others, is settled by proof before the commitment is made.
sessions.caseStudy:
Suppose a quiet woman who has said little for weeks finally speaks in the fifth session. She came certain that faith meant believing without evidence, and the study hasn't changed her mind about the evidence so much as about the word. She's noticed that she trusts her husband of thirty years without proof he'll never betray her, and trusts her memory and the world without proof, and has never demanded certainty for those the way she demands it here.

The host doesn't rush to close anything. He asks the question the session ends on: is her hesitation about the strength of the evidence, or about what she'd have to do if it were true? She's quiet for a long moment and says she isn't sure, and that not being sure is the truest thing she's said in a long time.

She leaves still weighing, eyes open. The host, who promised no trick, lets her go with no pressure at all, which is part of why she might come back.

memoryVerse.text: Now faith is the assurance of things hoped for, the conviction of things not seen.

leaderPrimer:
Someone at your table is waiting for you to flinch. They may not know it, but they've watched Christians answer hard questions before, and what they remember isn't the answer. It's the moment the eyes went elsewhere, the pivot to a memorized line, the small evasion that said the question wasn't really welcome. That's the hazard in this room. Not the objections, which are printed in this guide and have been argued over for centuries, but the flinch. The skeptic across from you isn't mainly testing arguments. They're testing you.

Nobody is argued into the kingdom by losing a debate. A believer who doesn't panic when pushed tells a skeptic something an argument can't. When a question lands that you can't answer, say so, write it down, and come back next week having looked. That will do more for your credibility than a polished reply. Don't defend God as if he were fragile, and don't fill silence with certainty you don't have.

Thank people for hard questions, and help them sharpen an objection before you respond to it. Never shame a question, whether it's aggressive, familiar or feels like a test.

Watch the friend who did the inviting. They're often the most anxious person present, wincing at every hard question and tempted to jump in with a quick answer. Give them permission to relax, and gently slow them down if they rush.

The sessions build from the existence of God to the resurrection to the step of faith itself, and the last one asks for nothing except clarity about where the evidence leaves each person. Resist every urge to close the sale. There's no altar call in this study, and if you slip one in, the room will remember the bait-and-switch longer than anything else you said. Your work is to make Christianity discussable by serious adults, some for the first time. If a skeptic leaves unconvinced but no longer able to say that believing is stupid, the door stays open.

faq.q: Is this study a setup to get me to convert?
faq.a: No. There's no emotional ambush in the last session and no moment when you're pressed to decide. Each session states the strongest case against Christianity first, and the responses are allowed to be incomplete. The final session says plainly that the evidence points without proving, and that you're welcome to leave still weighing. Hosts are asked never to make conversion the goal of the evening, because the moment they do, the conversation becomes manipulation.

faq.q: Do I have to believe in God already to take part?
faq.a: No. The study is built for people who don't believe, or aren't sure, and are willing to look. You aren't expected to pray, agree or pretend. You're only asked to do what any serious person does: take the evidence and the objections both at full strength.

faq.q: Will my questions be treated as attacks?
faq.a: No. Hosts are asked never to shame a question, to thank the person, and often to help sharpen the objection before answering it. If you were raised in the faith and left over a question nobody would let you ask, this is meant to be a different room.

faq.q: Does the study claim to prove Christianity is true?
faq.a: No. It claims the evidence points, not that it compels. Fine-tuning and the moral argument make a personal universe a serious option without proving God. The case for the resurrection is presented as strong but not as a knockdown. The final session says that what remains is a step, the same kind people take in every important commitment. Overclaiming is treated as part of the problem.

faq.q: What if the host doesn't know the answer to my question?
faq.a: Then the host should say so. The study is built to be led by someone who isn't an expert. "I don't know, let me find out" and "here's who has written well on that" build trust. The study names thinkers on both sides, believers and skeptics, so you can read them for yourself.

faq.q: Why does each session put the objections before the answers?
faq.a: Because answering a weak version of an objection convinces no one who holds the strong one, and because stating someone's case fairly is basic integrity. The study gives the multiverse, the warfare story, the legend theory, the natural explanations of the empty tomb and the charge that faith ignores evidence their strongest form. Often the response grants part of the objection rather than defeating all of it.

faq.q: Is this going to be a science-versus-faith fight?
faq.a: Not the way you might expect. Session two argues that the famous war between science and faith is largely an inherited story. It grants that the church has at times resisted knowledge, separates what science establishes from the philosophy sometimes carried in with it, and agrees that the "god of the gaps" is a bad argument believers should reject too.

faq.q: The resurrection seems impossible. Why treat it as a historical question?
faq.a: Because Christianity insists on it. Paul wrote that if the resurrection didn't happen the faith is worthless. Session four grants that dead people stay dead, which is why a resurrection would be a miracle and why the first witnesses didn't believe it either. It then separates the historical question of what best explains the facts most scholars grant from the philosophical question of whether a miracle is possible at all.

faq.q: Isn't faith just believing things without evidence?
faq.a: There's a kind of religion that means exactly that, and the study agrees it has earned the criticism. But in its serious sense faith means trust extended beyond strict proof on the basis of evidence that points, which is how everyone lives in every important matter. You trust that the world is real, that your memory works, that the people you love aren't deceiving you. None of that is provable, and all of it is reasonable.

faq.q: What if I finish the study and still don't believe?
faq.a: Then you leave still weighing, and there are no hard feelings. The study doesn't promise to produce belief and refuses to manufacture a decision at the end. It hopes you'll have asked the questions with your mind fully engaged, taken the evidence and the objections seriously, and found the question that's really yours.

faq.q: I'm the believer who invited a skeptical friend. How do I keep from making it worse?
faq.a: Resist the urge to rescue the faith with a quick answer when your friend raises something you can't fully meet. Let the objections stand at full strength. Be willing to say in front of your friend that you don't know, or that you've wrestled with the same thing. Your candor will do more for them than a defense. You did a good thing by inviting them. The harder good thing is to let the room be safe.

faq.q: Why does the writer keep naming his own wants and the believers' biases?
faq.a: Because everyone's wants bend what they're willing to look at, skeptics' and believers' alike, and naming that pull is where clear thinking starts. A study that pointed only at the skeptic's biases would be one-sided, and fairness is the whole wager here.

timeline.event: At his trial in Athens, as Plato records it, Socrates says that the unexamined life is not worth living.
Jesus of Nazareth is crucified under the Roman prefect Pontius Pilate, an event most historians, believing and skeptical, treat as among the most certain facts of ancient history.
Paul writes 1 Corinthians and passes on a creed about Jesus' death, burial, resurrection and appearances that many scholars date to within a few years of the crucifixion.
The four Gospels are written, on most scholars' dating, within the lifetime of people who could remember the events.
The Roman historian Tacitus records that Christ suffered the death penalty under Pontius Pilate in the reign of Tiberius.
Thomas Aquinas writes the Summa Theologiae, including his arguments from causation and contingency toward the existence of God.
David Hume publishes "Of Miracles" in An Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding, framing the strongest objection taken up in session four.
Charles Darwin publishes On the Origin of Species, a natural account of the diversity of life that reshapes the conversation between science and faith.
John William Draper and Andrew Dickson White publish the books that fixed the "warfare" of science and religion in the popular mind, a thesis later historians of science largely set aside.
W. K. Clifford's "The Ethics of Belief" demands sufficient evidence for every belief; William James answers in The Will to Believe.
C. S. Lewis, a convert from atheism, gives the wartime BBC talks later gathered as Mere Christianity (1952), including the moral argument and his challenge to the "great teacher" view of Jesus.
Physicists increasingly discuss how finely balanced several fundamental constants are for a universe with observers; Brandon Carter names the "anthropic principle" in 1973.
Alvin Plantinga develops the argument that belief in God can be rational without proof, from God and Other Minds (1967) to Warranted Christian Belief (2000).
N. T. Wright publishes major volumes placing Jesus within first-century Judaism, ending with The Resurrection of the Son of God (2003).

Gary Habermas and Michael Licona set out the minimal facts approach (2004); Richard Bauckham argues for eyewitness testimony behind the Gospels (2006); Licona publishes his longer historical study (2010).

facilitatorScript.open: Welcome, and thanks for being here, especially if you walked in skeptical; that took more nerve than walking in convinced. A few promises before we start. First, there's no trick in this study. There's no ambush in the last session and no moment when you're pressed to decide anything. You can leave wherever you land, with no hard feelings. Second, every hard question is welcome, the sharper the better, and nobody's question will be treated as an attack. If you have a doubt, say it at full strength. Third, I'm not the expert. I won't know plenty of the answers, and when I don't, I'll say so and point you to people who've studied the question. Tonight we're asking this together: ________. Let me read our passage, and then let's put the hardest version of tonight's question on the table.
facilitatorScript.transition: We've stated the objection at full strength and weighed a response, and we've let the response be as incomplete as the truth requires. Now let's ask what it means for the way each of us actually thinks and lives.
facilitatorScript.close: We'll stop there, and notice we haven't tied a bow on it, because on questions this large the evidence points without proving, and pretending otherwise would break the promise we made. Take the question home with you. Read the passages if you want to, and spend some time with the reflection questions. Wherever you are tonight, more convinced, more skeptical or simply clearer, that's a good place to be, because you asked the question instead of inheriting the answer. I'll offer a short prayer to close, and you're welcome to listen as a guest.

cadences.name: The full study (8 weeks)
plan: Week 1: Orientation. Read the summary together, agree on no tricks and no shamed questions, and walk slowly through session 1's opening question. Say plainly that the study claims evidence that points, not proof.
Week 2: Session 1, Is There Anyone There, full discussion of fine-tuning and the moral argument, with care not to overclaim.
Week 3: Session 2, Hasn't Science Buried God, with extended time on the history of the supposed war and the category error.
Week 4: Session 3, Who Was Jesus, Really, part one through the sources and the claims Jesus made about himself.
Week 5: Session 3 continued, the trilemma and the legend theory weighed against the early dating of the high claims.
Week 6: Session 4, Did the Resurrection Happen, the minimal facts and the natural explanations taken one at a time.
Week 7: Session 4 continued, Hume's objection and the role of the prior, plus the resurrection accounts read side by side.
Week 8: Session 5, The Leap That Is Not Blind, faith as warranted trust and the honest naming of where each person stands.

cadences.name: The intensive (4 weeks)
plan: Week 1: Sessions 1 and 2 together, whether anyone is there and whether science buried the question.
Week 2: Session 3, Who Was Jesus, Really, the claims and the trilemma and the legend theory.
Week 3: Session 4, Did the Resurrection Happen, the minimal facts and the natural explanations weighed.
Week 4: Session 5, The Leap That Is Not Blind, plus a short honest close that names where each person actually stands.

cadences.name: As written (5 weeks)
plan: Week 1: Session 1, Is There Anyone There.
Week 2: Session 2, Hasn't Science Buried God.
Week 3: Session 3, Who Was Jesus, Really.
Week 4: Session 4, Did the Resurrection Happen.
Week 5: Session 5, The Leap That Is Not Blind.

bibliography.title: Mere Christianity
bibliography.author: C. S. Lewis
bibliography.note: From wartime BBC talks, published as a book in 1952. Lewis, a convert from atheism, opens with the moral argument (session 1) and challenges the "great teacher" view of Jesus (session 3).

bibliography.title: The Reason for God: Belief in an Age of Skepticism
bibliography.author: Timothy Keller
bibliography.note: Published in 2008. A pastor's treatment of the leading objections to Christianity that states the skeptic's case fairly before answering. Useful across all five sessions.

bibliography.title: Reasonable Faith: Christian Truth and Apologetics
bibliography.author: William Lane Craig
bibliography.note: A rigorous defense of the cosmological, fine-tuning and moral arguments and the historical case for the resurrection. Background for sessions 1 and 4. Read it for the arguments, not as a script.

bibliography.title: Warranted Christian Belief
bibliography.author: Alvin Plantinga
bibliography.note: Published in 2000. Plantinga's major argument that belief in God can be rational without proof. The philosophical backbone of session 5. Demanding but worth it.

bibliography.title: The Resurrection of the Son of God
bibliography.author: N. T. Wright
bibliography.note: Published in 2003. A large historical study arguing that the empty tomb and the appearances together, set against first-century Jewish belief, are best explained by an actual resurrection. Sessions 3 and 4.

bibliography.title: Jesus and the Eyewitnesses: The Gospels as Eyewitness Testimony
bibliography.author: Richard Bauckham
bibliography.note: Published in 2006. Argues that the Gospels rest on named eyewitness testimony rather than anonymous tradition, which bears on the legend theory in session 3.

bibliography.title: The Case for the Resurrection of Jesus
bibliography.author: Gary Habermas and Michael Licona
bibliography.note: Published in 2004. The accessible statement of the minimal facts method, building only on data most scholars grant. The method behind session 4.

bibliography.title: An Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding, section 10, "Of Miracles"
bibliography.author: David Hume
bibliography.note: Published in 1748. The classic argument against belief in miracles. Read it directly so the strongest objection in session 4 is met at full strength.

bibliography.title: Surprised by Joy
bibliography.author: C. S. Lewis
bibliography.note: Published in 1955. Lewis's account of his long, reluctant road from atheism to faith. Background for the whole study.

bibliography.title: The Will to Believe
bibliography.author: William James
bibliography.note: A lecture published in 1896, answering the demand that belief always wait for sufficient evidence. A clarifying voice for session 5.

bibliography.title: How Jesus Became God
bibliography.author: Bart Ehrman
bibliography.note: Published in 2014. A widely read skeptical scholar who grants core historical facts while withholding the supernatural conclusion. Included so the leader hears the skeptical case from one of its ablest representatives.

bibliography.title: Letters to a Diminished Church and broader essays
bibliography.author: Dorothy L. Sayers
bibliography.note: A posthumous collection of Sayers's essays on taking the content of the creeds seriously rather than sentimentally. Background across the sessions.

furtherReading: The Reason for God, Timothy Keller, for a fuller pass through the leading objections, handled fairly.
Mere Christianity, C. S. Lewis, for the moral argument and his challenge to the "great teacher" view of Jesus.
The Case for the Resurrection of Jesus, Gary Habermas and Michael Licona, for the minimal facts method behind session 4.
"Of Miracles" in Hume's Enquiry, to meet the strongest objection to the resurrection in its original form before reading replies.
Surprised by Joy, C. S. Lewis, for what coming to belief looked like for one serious mind that resisted it for a long time.

glossary.definition: Here, someone who doesn't believe Christianity's central claims, or isn't sure of them, and weighs claims by evidence and argument. The study treats the skeptic as a serious thinker, not an opponent.

The observation that several fundamental constants of physics sit in narrow ranges that permit a universe with observers. The study treats it as a fact that calls for explanation, not as a proof of God.
The argument that our conviction that some things are really wrong, not merely disliked, is hard to ground in a purely material universe and fits more naturally if reality is personal.
Invoking God only to explain what science hasn't yet explained, so that God shrinks with each discovery. The study rejects it; the Christian claim is that God grounds the whole order.
C. S. Lewis's argument that a man who said what Jesus said can't be merely a great moral teacher. It assumes Jesus made the claims, which the legend theory disputes.
The view that the divine claims about Jesus grew gradually after his death. The study weighs it against how early and how Jewish the highest claims already are.
An approach to the resurrection associated with Gary Habermas that argues only from data most scholars grant, then asks what best explains it.
How likely a person thinks a claim is before examining the specific evidence. Someone whose starting point against miracles is absolute has settled the resurrection question in advance.

The study's description of faith in its serious sense: trust extended beyond strict proof toward what the evidence makes reasonable, the same kind of commitment people make in marriage and friendship.
Alvin Plantinga's term for a belief that can be rationally held as a starting point rather than as the conclusion of an argument, as belief in other minds is.
Reasoning toward God from the world and ordinary human experience rather than from Scripture. Fine-tuning and the moral argument belong to it.
The assumption that nothing outside nature can act within it, so that no event like a resurrection could happen whatever the evidence. A philosophical commitment, not a scientific result.
To state an opposing argument in its strongest form before responding, the opposite of attacking a caricature. This study asks hosts to do it every session.

promoKit.bulletinBlurb: Many studies for skeptics are sales pitches in disguise, and thoughtful people can tell. This one isn't. Over five sessions it asks whether Christianity is true and means the question: whether anyone is there, whether science buried God, who Jesus was, whether the resurrection happened, and what kind of step faith is. Each session states the hardest objection first. It claims evidence that points, not proof, and it never shames a question. A host who isn't an expert can lead it. Come skeptical. There's no trick.
